judge_assessment.explanation: The one-output-per-input reasoning is applied correctly everywhere and I checked each item: 3 arrows against 3 inputs (=) in problem 1 with the input 4 sending to 5; 4 arrows against 3 inputs (<) in problem 2 with 3 as the offending input; 4 points against 4 first coordinates in problem 3 with 3(5)+1 = 16; |x| giving 3 at both -3 and 3 and passing the vertical line test; five readings against five hours in problem 5; the circle of radius 5 giving upper output 4 at x = 3 and failing the test; the reversed book relation having 4 arrows against 3 inputs; 3k = 12 giving k = 4; four points against three first coordinates in problem 9 with 2+3 = 5 confirming the line; and four students against four lockers in problem 10. Two artifact defects contradict the perfect scores for mathematical correctness and clarity, and both are in the delivered worksheet PDF. (1) Problem 3(b) reads 'Write the rule in the form y = 3x + 1 and use it to give the output when the input is 5.' The rule for {(1,4),(2,7),(3,10),(4,13)} IS y = 3x + 1, so the stem prints the answer to its own first request; the intended template was clearly y = mx + b. (2) Problem 5's table prints Hour 1..5 with Temp 8, 10, blank, 15, 15 - the hour-3 cell is empty in worksheet.tex and in the compiled PDF - while part (a) asks 'Give the temperature at hour 3'. The answer key then says 'Reading down the hour row to 3 and across gives 12', describing a table cell that does not exist; 12 is only obtainable from the line plot beneath. verify.json id 5 declares data {'1':8,'2':10,'3':12,'4':15,'5':15} with the note 'read from the table and confirmed on the plot', so the JSON holds a given the worksheet never printed. Separately, the Quick Answers bank drops eight of ten rows' relations ('1. 5, -', '2. -', '3. -, 16', '5. 12, -', '6. 4, -', '7. 4, 7, -', '9. -, 5', '10. 214, -') on a sheet whose method is literally 'write the two counts with <, > or = between them', and problems 2 and 9(b) print identification slots ('name the input that spoils it', 'say which single point you would delete') with no manual entry.

strengths_to_preserve: One test is taught and then applied in seven different representations - mapping diagram, plotted set, absolute-value graph, table plus line plot, circle, bar chart reversed into a relation, and a student-to-locker diagram - and the count test is stated identically in the directions, in every stem and in the study guide ('count the pairs, count the different inputs, compare'). The consistency is what makes the vertical line test land as the same idea rather than a second rule.

Problem 8 turns the definition into an equation: the input 2 has two arrows, so the diagram can only be a function if 3k = 12, and the student solves for k = 4. That is the one item that tests whether the student can use the definition rather than recognise it, and verify.json backs it with a real solve entry.

Problem 7 reverses a bar chart into a relation (books as inputs, readers as outputs) so that the same data is a function in one direction and not in the other - Ana and Cy both read 7 - which is the cleanest possible demonstration that 'outputs may repeat, inputs may not' is a statement about direction.

The manual entries on problems 4, 6 and 10 are declared where they belong and carry objective criteria: problem 4(c) asks why two inputs sharing an output is harmless while one input with two outputs is fatal, and the key's model answer names the failure test ('asking "what is the output at 3?" would have two answers, and the vertical line x = 3 would cut the graph twice').

root_causes.description: Two authoring defects survived every gate. Problem 3(b) uses the instance's own answer as its format example, so the stem gives away the rule it asks for. Problem 5's table is missing the hour-3 cell that the problem, the answer key and verify.json all assume is printed - the value exists in the verify JSON's data dict and on the plot, but not in the table the key tells the student to read.
evidence: worksheet.pdf page 2, problem 3: 'Write the rule in the form y = 3x + 1 and use it to give the output when the input is 5', for the relation {(1,4),(2,7),(3,10),(4,13)} whose rule is y = 3x + 1.
worksheet.tex problem 5 table row: '$8$ & $10$ & & $15$ & $15$' - an empty cell - confirmed blank in the compiled worksheet.pdf.
answer_key.tex problem 5: 'Reading down the hour row to 3 and across gives 12, and the plotted point at hour 3 sits at the same height.'
verify.json id 5: data {'1': 8, '2': 10, '3': 12, '4': 15, '5': 15} with note 'Temperature at hour 3, read from the table and confirmed on the plot'.

root_causes.description: The prose-consistency gate is one-directional. It reports numbers that appear in the printed problem but not in the JSON, so it cannot see a given that the JSON declares and the worksheet omits - exactly the hour-3 defect. gate_log.txt even reports 'problem 5: 8 prose numbers ok' for the problem whose table is missing a value.
evidence: gate_log.txt step 20: 'problem 5: 8 prose numbers  ok' while the printed table lacks the 12 that verify.json's data dict contains.
The same report lists only 'missing from JSON' directions for problems 3, 6 and 8; there is no 'missing from worksheet' direction at all.
All 22 gates report PASS and the build ends 'BUILD PASSED', with the missing cell invisible to every one of them.

root_causes.description: render_quick_answers._fmt sympifies string expecteds, so every compare relation raises and prints '---'. On this sheet the count comparison IS the answer to the central sub-part of nearly every problem, so eight of ten bank rows lose their relation and three rows ('2. -' and the leading dashes on 3 and 9) carry no usable information at all.
evidence: gate_log.txt records PASS for all eight compare entries (e.g. 'Problem 2: compare(3 vs 4) -> < (expected <)').
answer_key.tex boxes those same relations correctly in the worked solutions ('3 = 3', '3 < 4', '4 = 4', '5 = 5').
Problems 4, 6 and 10 carry genuine manual entries, so the em-dash means two different things on the same page.

improvements.title: A 'write it in the form ...' template must use generic parameters, never the instance's own coefficients
improvements.proposed_change: Fix problem 3(b) to read 'Write the rule in the form y = mx + b', and add a gate check that fails the build when a problem's printed stem contains the literal text of that problem's own boxed answer. The check can compare each worksheet problem block against the \ans content bound to the same id by check_answer_key.py, normalising whitespace and math spacing. State the rule in SKILL.md next to the guidance on worked examples: format templates are written with generic parameters (mx + b, ax^2 + bx + c), because an instance-specific template hands over the answer.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture pairing this worksheet's problem 3 stem ('Write the rule in the form y = 3x + 1 ...') with an answer key whose problem 3 boxes y = 3x + 1. The new check must exit non-zero naming the leaked answer; changing the stem to 'in the form y = mx + b' must make it pass. Today no gate inspects the stem against the key's boxed answers, so the check fails to exist rather than fails to fire.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes a sub-part that cannot assess anything - the student copies the rule out of the question - and prevents the same slip on every 'write it in the form ...' item across the suite.
improvements.risk: A stem that legitimately restates a given (problem 1 of curr-211 prints 'Equation: 3x + 2 = x + 8' on purpose) could trip the check, so it must compare against the boxed ANSWER only and allow an explicit opt-out field for model-reading problems that supply the equation deliberately.

improvements.title: Make the prose-consistency gate check the reverse direction: every JSON given must be printed
improvements.proposed_change: Extend tests/check_prose_consistency.py to report, per problem, any value in the entry's givens (read_data 'data', eval 'at', system coefficients, compare 'values') that does not appear anywhere in that problem's printed block or its figure labels, and fail the build for read_data data in particular, since a data value the student cannot see makes the question unanswerable. Fix this case by restoring the 12 in problem 5's table.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: this worksheet's problem 5 block (table with the blank hour-3 cell) plus verify.json id 5's data {'1':8,'2':10,'3':12,'4':15,'5':15}. The reverse check must exit non-zero naming the unprinted key '3' -> 12. Restoring the cell makes it pass. Today the gate log reports 'problem 5: 8 prose numbers ok' for exactly this input, so the assertion fails before the fix.
improvements.expected_impact: Catches the class of defect where an artifact repair or a hand edit drops a table cell or a figure label while the JSON still carries the value - invisible to every current gate, and directly answerable-versus-unanswerable for the student.
improvements.risk: Givens that are deliberately hidden (a value the student must derive, a distractor held back) would trip the check, so the entry needs an opt-out field such as "hidden_givens": ["3"] rather than a blanket failure.

improvements.title: Restore the count comparisons that blank eight of ten rows on this bank
improvements.proposed_change: Handle relation strings in render_quick_answers._fmt before sympify, printing the operator between the entry's compared values (id 2 -> '3 < 4'), and keep '---' only for ids whose entries are all manual - which matters especially here, where problems 4, 6 and 10 have real manual entries and their rows are indistinguishable from the dropped relations.
improvements.regression_test: Render this task's verify.json and assert that ids 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9 and 10 all contain a relation operator in their rows, and that row 2 in particular is not '---'. Today eight rows carry the em-dash, so the assertion fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: This is the worst instance of the bug in the batch: the sheet's stated method is comparing two counts, and the grading page currently prints that comparison for none of the ten problems.
improvements.risk: Rows such as '3 = 3' are short, so the layout risk here is negligible.

improvements.title: Flag the 'name the input that spoils it' and 'which point would you delete' slots as manual
improvements.proposed_change: Add the open-response and named-error scan to the gate chain so problem 2 ('If it is not, name the input that spoils it'), problem 9(b) ('say which single point you would delete to repair the relation') and problem 6(c) ('justify it by naming a vertical line that meets the graph twice') each carry a manual entry, matching the treatment problems 4, 6 and 10 already receive.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture with problem 2's stem and a verify.json id 2 holding only the compare entry. The check must exit non-zero naming the 'name the input that spoils it' slot; adding a manual entry makes it pass. The key already states the expected answer ('The input that spoils it is 3: it sends to 6 and to 8'), so the desc is available.
improvements.expected_impact: Naming the offending input is what the key itself calls the proof ('"Not a function" without naming it is only half an answer'), and it currently reaches no reviewer.
improvements.risk: The sheet already has three manual items; adding two or three more is a real review-load increase on a ten-problem worksheet, which is the intended trade.

case_summary: A varied and conceptually consistent introduction to deciding whether a relation is a function - one count test applied across seven representations, a genuine use-the-definition item in problem 8 (3k = 12 gives k = 4), a bar chart reversed so the same data is a function in one direction only, and three properly declared manual explanations. But two content defects reached the delivered PDFs. Problem 3(b) says 'Write the rule in the form y = 3x + 1' for a relation whose rule is y = 3x + 1, so the stem prints its own answer where 'y = mx + b' belonged. And problem 5's table is missing the hour-3 temperature entirely, while the problem asks for it, the answer key says to read it from the table, and verify.json declares it as data - the value exists everywhere except on the page the student sees. No gate could catch the second one because the prose-consistency check only looks for printed numbers missing from the JSON, never the reverse. On top of that, the Quick Answers bank drops the count comparison from eight of ten rows on a worksheet whose method is comparing two counts, and two identification slots are recorded as machine-verified.
